clue.text: Result implying down is cold?

parts.note: surface reading: an outcome suggesting that the downstairs or the feathers are chilly
setter's reading: if down is cold, then by implication the opposite direction is warm, a phrase that runs together as one word

explanation.surface: Someone draws a conclusion that the downstairs, or the duvet, is chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: If down is cold, then UP'S HOT, which read as one word is UPSHOT.
explanation.definitionFit: An upshot is the final outcome or consequence of events, a plain synonym for result.

clue.text: Cannon in castle, say

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a gun or artillery weapon
second meaning: a chessman, of which the rook or castle is one example

explanation.surface: A big gun mounted inside a fortress.
explanation.definitionFit: A field gun is called an artillery piece, and a chess castle is one of the pieces on the board.

clue.text: Taking map, had set out for city area

indicators.note: out here means put out of place, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone takes a map and heads off to explore a district of the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set out' reads as a phrase meaning departed, but set is part of the letters and out alone says rearrange. Hampstead is a district of north London.
explanation.definitionFit: Hampstead is a leafy residential district of north London, an area within the capital.

clue.text: Producer of scores with no end of elegance

indicators.note: with no end of says one word loses the final letter of the other

parts.note: tallies are running scores or counts
the final letter of elegance

explanation.surface: A writer of music lacking any finesse.
explanation.walkthrough: Scores works twice: as musical scores in the definition and as tallies in the wordplay. Thomas Tallis was a Tudor composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Tallis was an English Tudor composer of church music, so he produced musical scores.

clue.text: Odd card received in iona, perhaps, from another islander

indicators.note: odd means strange or irregular, so the letters are put out of their normal order
perhaps hints that the island's name too could be spelt some other way

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; the Hebridean island also prompts the islander theme

explanation.surface: A strange playing card turns up on Iona, sent by someone from a different island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'received in iona, perhaps' tells you the word card goes in with Iona's letters before both are mixed; 'perhaps' warns that Iona's letters too are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: An Orcadian is a native of Orkney, so a different islander from someone living on Iona.

clue.text: More demanding student craftsman becomes an author

parts.note: Oliver Twist, the workhouse boy who famously asked for more
a goldsmith is an artisan who works precious metal

explanation.surface: A student who wants more becomes a craftsman and then turns writer.
explanation.walkthrough: More demanding looks like a comparative adjective, but it means demanding more, as Dickens's Oliver did.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver Goldsmith was the eighteenth-century Irish writer of The Vicar of Wakefield and She Stoops to Conquer.

clue.text: One who enjoys watching from nice seat, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters could be ordered some other way

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A spectator enjoys the view from a comfortable seat.
explanation.definitionFit: A cineaste is a devotee of films, an enthusiast who loves watching cinema.

clue.text: Mostly thrive as joiner employed by carpenter

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to do well is to thrive

explanation.surface: A carpenter's apprentice mostly prospers as a joiner.
explanation.walkthrough: Joiner looks like a tradesman, but here it is the thing that joins two pieces of wood.
explanation.definitionFit: A dowel is a wooden peg used by woodworkers to join two pieces together.

clue.text: Dismay about artist is seen in value judgment

indicators.note: about means going around, so one word wraps the others

parts.note: to appal is to fill with dismay
RA, Royal Academician
taken as written

explanation.surface: A critic's horror at a painter shows in the assessment.
explanation.definitionFit: An appraisal is an evaluation or assessment of worth, a considered judgment of value.

clue.text: in a rare appearance, Red's opposed to monarch a great deal

parts.note: surface padding that flags an unusual spelling of the colour, with a doubled consonant
V is short for versus, against
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
a million is a very large amount

explanation.surface: A rarely seen Red politician takes a firm stand against the monarchy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a rare appearance' warns that the answer uses an unusual spelling: the colour is normally written with one L.
explanation.definitionFit: Vermilion is a brilliant scarlet pigment, so it is a shade of red.

clue.text: Did keen partners briefly part?

indicators.note: briefly asks for the word to be cut short, here reduced to its abbreviation

parts.note: West and East are partners at the bridge table
PT is the standard abbreviation for part

explanation.surface: A question whether two eager partners split up.
explanation.walkthrough: Keen here is a verb, to wail in mourning, not the adjective eager.
explanation.definitionFit: To keen is to lament loudly over the dead, so having keened means having cried or wailed.

clue.text: Targets set by party in North-East area

parts.note: golf tees are what a golfer places the ball on, the targets of the swing
a side is one party in a dispute or game

explanation.surface: A political party sets its election targets in north-east England.
explanation.walkthrough: Teesside is the industrial region around the River Tees in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Teesside is the region of north-east England around Middlesbrough on the River Tees.

clue.text: Solvent, with a little money for starting business

parts.note: taken as written
a float is the small sum of cash put in a till at the start of trading

explanation.surface: A start-up stays in the black with only a small amount of seed capital.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm that is afloat is financially sound, able to pay its debts, which is what solvent means.

clue.text: Affectedly dainty in what we eat

indicators.note: in tells you the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: letters running across the end of what, all of we, and the start of eat

explanation.surface: Our food is fussily dainty.
explanation.definitionFit: Twee is a British word for something excessively quaint, cute or sentimental, overly precious in manner.

clue.text: Way in which government departments are grouped

definitions.text: Way in which government departments are grouped

parts.words: Way in which government departments are grouped
parts.note: surface reading: the method by which ministries are organised
setter's reading: way is a street, the London road lined with ministries

explanation.walkthrough: Way looks like a manner or method, but it is a road: Whitehall is the London street of government offices.
explanation.definitionFit: Whitehall is the Westminster thoroughfare lined with ministry buildings, and its name stands for the civil service.

clue.text: Supporter at entrance privy to our secrets?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the upright on which a gate hangs
second meaning: the idiom 'between you, me and the' this post, said when sharing a confidence

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'between you, me and the gatepost' introduces a secret, so the post is treated as the third party who hears it.
explanation.definitionFit: A gatepost holds up a gate at an entrance, and is the silent third party in a familiar idiom for confidences.

clue.text: Showing equipment and plan to ordinary soldiers

parts.note: to project is to plan
OR, other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Display gear and a scheme for the rank and file.
explanation.definitionFit: A projector is the apparatus used to show films or slides on a screen.

clue.text: Swift character was placed here in short race

definitions.text: Swift character was placed here in short race

parts.words: Swift character was placed here in short race
parts.note: surface reading: a fast runner ran in a sprint
setter's reading: Jonathan Swift's hero Gulliver, set down among a race of tiny people

explanation.walkthrough: Swift is the author Jonathan Swift, and short race means a race of tiny people, not a sprint: Gulliver was washed up in LILLIPUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Lilliput is the island of minute inhabitants where Gulliver lands in Swift's satire Gulliver's Travels.

clue.text: Theatre of war

parts.note: surface reading: an arena where military operations take place
setter's reading: a London theatre famous for staying open throughout the Blitz

explanation.walkthrough: The Windmill Theatre in Soho boasted 'We never closed', keeping its revues running through the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: The Windmill was the London theatre celebrated for performing throughout wartime bombing, so it is a theatre of the war.

clue.text: Slow-moving predators

indicators.note: moving suggests the letters are shifted about into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Hunting animals that move sluggishly.
explanation.walkthrough: Slow-moving reads as one adjective, but it splits into the letters and the instruction to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: Owls are birds of prey, hunting mice and other small creatures at night.

clue.text: Ornament 'arry put into French church

indicators.note: the dropped aitch shows the Cockney way of speaking, which loses the opening letter

parts.note: Harry is a form of Henry, which in French is Henri
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A Cockney called Harry decorates a church in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arry is Cockney Harry, a name for Henry; put into French that is Henri, and the Cockney drops its H.
explanation.definitionFit: To ornament something is to adorn it, and enrich can mean to decorate richly.

clue.text: Happen to see French force to both sides

parts.note: the British Expeditionary Force, the army sent to fight in France
everyone on both sides is all of them

explanation.surface: A French army happens to be seen pushing out to both flanks.
explanation.walkthrough: BEF, the British Expeditionary Force, was the army that went to France in both World Wars.
explanation.definitionFit: To befall is to happen, used especially of misfortune that comes upon someone.

clue.text: Insect a plant's head concealed

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of plant
hid means concealed

explanation.surface: A bug hidden at the top of a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: An aphid is a small sap-sucking insect such as the greenfly, a garden pest.

clue.text: It may be fine as a writing unit

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a punishment handed down by a court, which could be a monetary penalty
second meaning: a grammatical unit of prose ending in a full stop

explanation.surface: Praise for a nicely crafted piece of prose.
explanation.walkthrough: Fine looks like an adjective of praise, but it is the penalty paid in money.
explanation.definitionFit: A court's punishment may be a fine, and in grammar the same word names a complete group of words.

clue.text: Introduction of controls on game in part of Africa

indicators.note: an introduction is the opening, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of controls
taken as written
Go is the Japanese board game

explanation.surface: Rules imposed on hunting in an African region.
explanation.definitionFit: The Congo is a region of central Africa, named for its great river and the countries there.

clue.text: Get ready for hiding-place, say

indicators.note: say asks for the word as it is spoken rather than as it is written

parts.note: a cache is a hidden store

explanation.surface: Preparing a secret hideaway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is slang for ready money, so to get ready for a cheque is to turn it into money.
explanation.definitionFit: To cash a cheque is to exchange it for banknotes, which is getting ready money for it.

clue.text: Uncouth type in ship I let become disorderly

indicators.note: disorderly means out of order, so the letters lose their sequence

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A boor allowed aboard a ship turns rowdy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link telling you where the type is, but it is part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A philistine is someone hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts, a crude, uncultivated person.

clue.text: Chevalier's beloved language

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the wife celebrated in the music-hall song 'My ...' sung by Albert Chevalier
second meaning: the medieval form of the tongue spoken in the Netherlands

explanation.walkthrough: Chevalier is the Victorian music-hall star Albert Chevalier, not Maurice; 'old Dutch' is Cockney slang for one's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is old Cockney slang for a wife, made famous by Chevalier's song, and also the early medieval Dutch tongue.

clue.text: School that cultivates the upper crust

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a famous English public school in north-west London
second meaning: a farm implement that breaks up the surface soil

explanation.surface: A posh school grooms the aristocracy.
explanation.walkthrough: The upper crust is literally the top layer of soil, not just the social elite that the school educates.
explanation.definitionFit: A harrow is a frame of spikes dragged over ploughed land to break up the topsoil, and Harrow is an elite school.
